triage.rationale: Seasonal pruritus with paw licking and ventral erythema is consistent with allergic dermatitis; no systemic illness or acute distress reported.

Prior history of recurrent otitis externa suggests an underlying atopic/allergic dermatitis. Photo of the ventral abdomen shows erythema and hyperpigmentation without visible pustules or ulceration. No systemic signs (lethargy, anorexia, vomiting) are reported by the owner.

No pustules, papules, crusting, or ulceration are visible. Mammary glands appear otherwise unremarkable; a harness is present on the thorax.
pp-1001.clientCommunication: Thanks for sending photos and details about your dog's itching. It sounds like her skin flares up seasonally, and the rusty color between her toes is often just saliva staining from licking rather than a separate problem. We'd like to see her for an exam and some simple in-house skin tests to check for secondary infection or irritation and make sure her flea prevention is fully on track. In the meantime, please try to avoid any new soaps or lotions on her skin and keep up her flea/tick medication consistently, and let us know if she starts scratching more intensely, seems uncomfortable, or you notice any sores or odor.

limitations: No physical exam performed
Photo shows only ventral abdomen, not paws where owner reports primary staining
Cannot assess for secondary infection depth, odor, or exudate from photo alone
Owner-reported history of symptom timing and severity not independently verified
Breed listed as Labrador Retriever but coat pattern in photo appears merle-patterned, atypical for the breed, suggesting possible mismatch in submitted signalment

triage.rationale: Acute, painful, exudative skin lesion with self-trauma (head shaking) warrants exam and treatment within 24-48h to prevent worsening and address possible underlying otitis.

pp-1002.clinicalSummary: 6-year-old neutered male Golden Retriever presents with acute (overnight) onset of a well-demarcated, moist, erythematous, exudative lesion on the left ventral cheek/submandibular region following swimming, with associated pain on palpation and head shaking. Clinical picture is consistent with pyotraumatic dermatitis (hot spot), likely triggered by moisture retention in the dense coat and self-trauma from scratching or head shaking. Head shaking raises concern for concurrent otitis externa as an underlying pruritic trigger. No systemic signs (lethargy, anorexia, fever) reported by owner.

supporting: Rapid onset within 24 hours after swimming

Swimming is a common trigger for otitis externa

Moist environment predisposes to bacterial overgrowth

pp-1002.imageFindings: Well-demarcated, oval, alopecic, erythematous patch on the ventral cheek/submandibular skin with a moist, glistening, slightly eroded surface; surrounding hair is matted and discolored (likely serous/hemorrhagic exudate staining); margins are sharply defined against normal haired skin with no visible satellite lesions in frame.

pp-1002.clientCommunication: Thanks for sending the photo \u2014 it looks like your dog may have developed what's commonly called a 'hot spot,' a sore, moist skin irritation that can appear very quickly, especially after swimming or scratching. These can be quite uncomfortable, so please try to prevent him from further scratching or rubbing the area (an e-collar can help) until we can see him. We'd also like to check his ears since the head shaking could be a related issue. Please bring him in within the next day or two so we can clean the area, check for infection, and get him comfortable.

limitations: No physical examination performed
Ear canals not visualized to assess for otitis externa
No information on pruritus history, parasite prevention, or prior skin issues
Photo does not show full extent of lesion margins or surrounding skin

triage.rationale: History strongly suggests dermatophytosis (ringworm) with concurrent human infection, which is zoonotic and contagious among household pets and people, warranting prompt veterinary evaluation and containment.

pp-1003.clinicalSummary: Young adult spayed female DSH presents with owner-reported circular, alopecic, scaly lesions on the face and ears, occurring shortly after introduction of a kitten with similar lesions. A household member (child) has since developed an itchy, erythematous annular skin lesion, raising strong suspicion for zoonotic dermatophytosis (likely Microsporum canis). No prior dermatologic history is reported, and the cat is otherwise systemically well per owner account. Leading concern is contagious fungal dermatitis requiring confirmatory testing and household-wide management to limit further zoonotic and interspecies spread.

supporting: Concurrent similar lesions in a recently introduced kitten
New itchy annular (ring-shaped) lesion in a human household member
Classic distribution on face/ears with alopecia and scaling in a young cat
Indoor/outdoor and multi-pet household increase exposure risk
against: No photo or exam to confirm morphology, Wood's lamp or culture pending

Occasionally weakly zoonotic causing transient pruritic lesions in humans
against: Less common in indoor/outdoor pet populations in many regions
Pattern of spread to multiple household pets and a human ring-shaped lesion is more classic for dermatophytosis

against: Not contagious/zoonotic, so would not explain kitten or human lesions
Typically less pruritic and not classically annular

Round, ring-like lesion pattern is atypical for uncomplicated allergic or bacterial disease

pp-1003.clientCommunication: Thank you for the detailed history \u2014 the pattern you're describing (round bald, scaly patches on your cat and kitten, plus your daughter's itchy ring-shaped rash) is most consistent with a common, treatable fungal skin infection that can spread between pets and people. We'd like to see your cat soon so we can run a couple of quick, painless tests to confirm this and start the right treatment. In the meantime, it's a good idea to keep the affected pets separated from other animals and family members where possible, wash your hands after handling them, and have your daughter's rash checked by her doctor. This condition is very manageable once identified, and early treatment helps everyone in the household recover faster.

limitations: No physical examination performed
No photo available to characterize lesion morphology
Diagnosis based on owner-reported symptoms and secondary account of human lesion, not clinically verified

triage.rationale: A rapidly growing, fluctuating, red lump in a Boxer is suspicious for a mast cell tumor, which needs prompt sampling before any manipulation or removal.

pp-1004.clinicalSummary: 9-year-old neutered male Boxer with a solitary cutaneous/subcutaneous mass on the right lateral thorax that has grown from pea- to grape-sized over 3 weeks, with intermittent erythema and swelling ('waxing and waning' appearance consistent with possible Darier's sign). Boxers are a breed strongly predisposed to mast cell tumors, which can present exactly this way. No systemic signs (vomiting, inappetence, lethargy) are reported by the owner, but these should be specifically screened for at the visit. Prior history of benign lipomas does not rule out a new, biologically distinct mass.

supporting: Waxing/waning size and erythema (possible Darier's sign from mast cell degranulation)
Well-circumscribed, dome-shaped, erythematous, hairless nodule on photo
against: No documented ulceration or ecchymosis
Cannot assess firmness/mobility from photo alone
Typically younger dogs (<4 years)
Histiocytomas usually resolve rather than progressively enlarge over weeks

against: Lipomas are usually soft, slow-growing, and non-erythematous
Fluctuating redness/swelling is atypical for a simple lipoma

against: Persistent and progressively enlarging over 3 weeks rather than resolving

Avoid squeezing, biopsying without prior FNA, or repeated manipulation of the mass until mast cell tumor is ruled out, as this can trigger degranulation and systemic reaction
pp-1004.clientCommunication: Thank you for the clear photo and history — this is helpful. Because this lump has grown quickly and its redness/swelling seems to come and go, we'd like to see your dog soon (ideally within the next day or two) so we can take a small sample with a needle to look at under the microscope. This simple test is quick, usually doesn't require sedation, and gives us important information about what the lump is and how best to treat it. In the meantime, please try to avoid squeezing or rubbing the area.

limitations: No physical exam performed — mass consistency, mobility, and lymph node status unknown
Single photo only; lighting, angle, and lack of scale limit assessment of size and texture
Owner-reported growth timeline and symptom pattern are unverified
No cytology or histopathology results available yet

triage.rationale: Significant weight loss with excessive thirst, urination, and vomiting in a senior cat suggests a metabolic disease (e.g., thyroid, kidney, or diabetes) that needs prompt bloodwork before it progresses to a crisis.

pp-1005.clinicalSummary: 12-year-old male neutered Persian cat with 20% body weight loss over the past year (4.5kg to 3.6kg), accompanied by polyphagia, polydipsia/polyuria, intermittent vomiting, and a greasy, poorly groomed coat. This symptom complex (weight loss despite good appetite, PU/PD, vomiting, coat neglect) is classic for feline hyperthyroidism, but overlaps significantly with diabetes mellitus and chronic kidney disease, which may coexist in a geriatric cat. Persian breed confers additional risk for polycystic kidney disease. No physical exam or diagnostics have yet been performed; the degree of dehydration, hydration status, and metabolic stability are unknown.

pp-1005.clientCommunication: Thank you for the detailed description of your cat's symptoms — the weight loss, increased thirst, and change in his coat are important signs that we take seriously, especially given his age. These symptoms can be caused by a few different treatable conditions, most commonly involving the thyroid, kidneys, or blood sugar, but we'll need some bloodwork and a urine sample to know for sure. Please try to get him in for an exam and testing within the next day or two, and in the meantime keep an eye out for worsening vomiting, lethargy, or reluctance to eat. We're glad you reached out, and we'll work together to figure out what's going on.

limitations: No physical examination performed yet

triage.rationale: Localized skin fold pyoderma/dermatitis in a brachycephalic breed is uncomfortable but not acutely dangerous; can be scheduled within routine timeframe.

pp-1006.clientCommunication: Thanks for the detailed description — it sounds like your pup may have some irritation and mild infection in her skin folds, which is quite common in French Bulldogs with their wrinkly faces and curly tails. We'll want to take a close look at the folds and possibly do a quick skin swab to see what's causing the odor and redness so we can choose the right treatment (often a cleanser and topical medication). This isn't usually an emergency, but keeping the area clean and dry until her visit can help with comfort. Please let us know if you notice her scratching excessively, developing sores, or acting unwell, and we'll get her seen sooner.

triage.rationale: Male cat with 12+ hours of no urination, straining, and vomiting is highly suspicious for urethral obstruction — a life-threatening emergency.

pp-1007.clinicalSummary: 5-year-old male neutered Maine Coon presents with acute stranguria, pollakiuria-like litter box behavior, vocalizing, lethargy, and a single vomiting episode, with reported anuria for approximately 12 hours. History of self-limiting hematuria one year prior suggests prior feline lower urinary tract disease (FLUTD). The combination of anuria, vomiting, and lethargy in this signalment raises strong concern for urethral obstruction with possible early post-renal azotemia and hyperkalemia. This is a time-critical presentation requiring immediate physical exam (bladder palpation) and stabilization.

pp-1007.clientCommunication: Thank you for reaching out right away — what you're describing, especially the straining without producing urine, needs to be checked by a veterinarian immediately, as it could indicate a blocked bladder, which is a true emergency in male cats. Please bring your cat in as soon as possible, even if that means an emergency clinic tonight. In the meantime, try to keep him calm and avoid giving any food or water unless instructed. We know this is stressful, and we're here to help get him comfortable and cared for quickly.

limitations: No physical exam performed
Owner-reported urination history may be imprecise (may reflect partial rather than complete obstruction)
No photo or diagnostic results available to confirm findings
Duration and severity of vomiting not fully detailed

triage.rationale: Young dog with periocular/muzzle alopecia and mild pruritus is most consistent with demodicosis, a non-emergent but contagious-to-manage condition warranting scheduled workup.

Dermatophytosis and other ectoparasites (Sarcoptes) remain differentials given shelter exposure and zoonotic/contagious potential. No systemic signs reported.

pp-1008.clientCommunication: Thanks for bringing in these details about your new pup's skin! Patchy hair loss around the eyes and muzzle with mild itching in a young dog is often caused by a small skin mite or, less commonly, a fungal skin infection—both very treatable once we identify the exact cause. We'll want to do a simple skin scraping and possibly a fungal test at his visit to pinpoint what's going on and get him started on the right treatment. In the meantime, try to limit close contact with other pets in the household just as a precaution until we know more.

limitations: No photo submitted to visually assess lesion characteristics (scale, crusting, erythema)
